summary.text: Bats, the order Chiroptera, are winged mammals and the only mammals capable of true and sustained flight.
They account for about 20% of all classified mammal species, with at least 1,500 known species, second only to rodents.
Most bats eat insects, and they matter to ecosystems by pollinating flowers, dispersing seeds and controlling insect populations.

facts.label: Largest bats
facts.value: Flying foxes, up to a 1.6 m wingspan

facts.label: Name meaning
facts.value: Greek words for hand and wing

facts.label: Oldest complete skeletons
facts.value: About 52 million years old, from Wyoming

items.prompt: A park ranger explains how bats compare with other mammals when it comes to getting airborne. What does she say?

options.label: They glide, as several other mammals do, but cannot flap
They are the only mammals capable of true, sustained flight
They fly less skilfully than most birds
They fly only when hunting insects at night

items.explain: Bats are the only mammals capable of true and sustained flight, and they are more agile in flight than most birds.

items.prompt: A farmer builds roosting boxes for bats beside her fields. What benefit is she after?

options.label: They eat insect pests, so she can use fewer pesticides
Their dung attracts the insects that pollinate her crops
They scare off larger animals that eat her crops
They spread fruit seeds by feeding on her insects

items.explain: Bats consume insect pests, reducing the need for pesticides and other insect management measures.

items.prompt: Why might a disease spread easily through a bat colony?

options.label: Bats only live in caves, so germs build up inside them
Bats feed mostly on blood, which passes germs along
Their wing membranes hold germs that rub off on neighbours
Bats are mobile, social and long-lived, and naturally carry many pathogens

items.explain: Bats act as a natural reservoir for many pathogens and, being highly mobile, social and long-lived, can readily spread disease among themselves.

items.prompt: Researchers have found fossils for only a small share of bat genera. What explains the gap?

options.label: Bats' delicate skeletons do not fossilise well
Bats only appeared in the last few million years
Bats' bones dissolve in the caves where they roost
Most bat remains were eaten by scavengers

items.explain: The delicate skeletons of bats do not fossilise well; only about 12% of bat genera have been found in the fossil record.

items.prompt: A 52-million-year-old fossil bat had claws on all five fingers and short, broad wings. What does this early bat suggest?

options.label: Echolocation came first and made flight possible
It could fly faster and farther than later bats
Flight appeared before the ability to echolocate
Mammals learned to fly twice, in two bat lines

items.explain: Onychonycteris indicates flight evolved before echolocation, and its short, broad wings suggest it could not fly as fast or far as later bats.

items.prompt: An older idea claimed big fruit-eating bats were kin of primates, implying that taking to the air happened twice in mammals. What do genome studies say?

options.label: Fruit-eating bats and primates share a flying ancestor
All bats share a common ancestor and mammal flight arose once
Mammal flight arose twice but in the same bat family
Genomes cannot say anything about how flight arose

items.explain: Genomic studies contradict the flying primate hypothesis and strongly support the common ancestry of all bats and a single origin of mammal flight.

paragraphs.heading: Mammals that fly
paragraphs.text: Bats make up the order Chiroptera, a name built from Ancient Greek words for "hand" and "wing". They are the only mammals that can truly fly and keep on flying. Each wing is a set of long, spread-out fingers covered by a thin membrane called the patagium. With it, bats move through the air more nimbly than most birds.

paragraphs.heading: A huge family
paragraphs.text: With at least 1,500 known species, bats make up about 20% of every classified mammal species, a total beaten only by rodents. They are found in almost every region of the world. The smallest, Kitti's hog-nosed bat, is 29–33 mm long and weighs 2 g, which makes it one of the tiniest mammals alive. The biggest are the flying foxes: the giant golden-crowned flying fox reaches 1.5 kg and has a wingspan of 1.6 m.

paragraphs.heading: What bats eat
paragraphs.text: Most bats eat insects. Of the rest, most live on fruit or on nectar. A few feed on animals other than insects, and vampire bats feed on blood. Most bats are active at night, and many shelter in caves or other refuges, though nobody is sure whether they do this to escape predators.

paragraphs.heading: Why bats matter
paragraphs.text: In their ecosystems, bats pollinate flowers, spread seeds and keep insect numbers in check. By eating insect pests they cut the need for pesticides, and their dung, called guano, has been dug out of caves to use as fertiliser. Bats can draw tourists, and people in Africa, Asia, the Pacific and the Caribbean eat them. They are also a natural home for many disease-causing pathogens such as rabies, and because they are mobile, social and long-lived, they pass disease among themselves easily. That becomes a danger when people interact with them.

paragraphs.heading: Traces in stone
paragraphs.text: Bat skeletons are delicate and do not fossilise well; only about 12% of the bat genera that ever lived are thought to have turned up as fossils. The oldest known bat fossils, from 55–56 million years ago, are nothing but isolated teeth. The oldest complete skeletons, 52 million years old, were found in Wyoming. Two bats from the Messel Pit in Germany, 48 million years old, were the first fossil mammals whose colour was discovered: both were reddish-brown.

paragraphs.heading: Flight came first
paragraphs.text: One of the Wyoming bats, Onychonycteris finneyi, found in 2003, shows that flight evolved before the ability to echolocate. Unlike bats today, it had claws on all five fingers, and its longer hind legs and shorter forearms may have helped it climb. Its short, broad wings suggest its flights were slower and shorter than those of later bats. Genome studies strongly back the idea that all bats share common ancestry and that flight arose just once in mammals.
